name: Conduit Rat
description:
Conduit Rats are slender, flattened rodents — roughly 35–45 cm body length — whose skeletal structure has narrowed over generations of living inside electrical conduit pipes, junction boxes, and cable trunking. Their ribcages can compress laterally by nearly a third, allowing passage through conduit as narrow as 5 cm in diameter. The fur is sparse and fine, almost velvety, which reduces friction in tight passages. Most striking is their coloration: a mottled grey-orange that closely mimics aged PVC conduit and oxidized metal surfaces. The ears are small and folded flat, the whiskers extraordinarily long and sensitive — used to detect vibration, air pressure changes, and the electromagnetic hum of live cables.

Conduit Rats have developed a behavioral relationship with electrical infrastructure that borders on the symbiotic — though the infrastructure definitely does not benefit. They chew cable sheathing selectively, consuming the plasticizer compounds that leach from aging PVC insulation, which appear to have become a dietary requirement. Nests are built from stripped wire insulation, foam fragments, and shredded fiber optic casing. Colonies within junction boxes can cause cascading electrical faults over weeks or months, and their presence is often the actual cause of brownouts attributed to aging grid infrastructure in Tier 1–2 districts. They are largely non-aggressive toward humans but will defend nest sites.

Electricians and infrastructure maintenance crews in GLMZ have a complicated relationship with Conduit Rats. Finding a nest often means hours of rerouting and repair, but experienced crews know that a hot-rat colony in a conduit run is also a reliable indicator of which sections of cable are oldest and most degraded — the rats always find the softest sheathing first. Some maintenance workers keep informal logs of colony locations and use them as a kind of living fault-map. In certain Tier 1 neighborhoods, a working electrician who doesn't know where the sparkers are nesting is considered dangerously inexperienced.
diet: PVC plasticizer compounds, cable sheathing, foam insulation, small invertebrates found in conduit systems
notable_traits: Laterally compressible ribcage for conduit navigation
Dietary dependence on PVC plasticizer compounds
encounters: Rarely seen directly — most encounters are with evidence of their presence: stripped cable, droppings in junction boxes, the smell of chewed plastic. Electricians and infrastructure crews encounter them during maintenance. Occasionally emerge at night around external conduit access points. Will bite if cornered inside a tight space.
known_uses: Informal living fault-indicators for experienced electricians. Some crews pay Tier 1 kids small amounts (Φ 1–3) to report active nest sites. No food or material use recorded.
story_hooks: A series of blackouts in a mid-tier district is officially blamed on aging infrastructure, but an electrician notices the Conduit Rat nest patterns suggest something is drawing them to a specific building's cable run — something generating unusual EM output

A Conduit Rat colony has nested inside the walls of a corporate-leased server facility; the facility manager wants them removed quietly before an audit, but removal will require cutting power to servers that someone very powerful does not want powered down
